opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the scratchpad is useful, but it's a bit like asking someone to narrate their thought process out loud. What they say is often correlated with what's actually happening, but it isn't guaranteed to be the real causal story. Circuits let you look underneath that narration.

When we trace a circuit, we're asking: for this particular output, which internal features lit up, how did they connect to each other, and which ones actually mattered causally? You can intervene. You turn a feature off, or amplify it, and see whether the behavior changes. That's a very different kind of evidence from reading text the model chose to write.

A few things come out of that. One is that you can see multi-step reasoning happening internally, within a single forward pass, without any of it showing up in the chain of thought. Take a question where you need to resolve an intermediate fact before you can answer. You can sometimes find the representation of that intermediate fact sitting in the middle layers and feeding into the final answer. The model is doing the hop internally.

Another is planning. Even in something like writing a rhyming line, you can find evidence that the model has already settled on where it's heading before it writes the words that lead there. So the computation isn't purely token-by-token improvisation, even though that's how the output looks.

The third, which I think matters most for safety, is that you can catch cases where the written reasoning and the internal computation come apart. The model might write out a plausible-looking derivation, but the circuit shows it was really working backward from an answer it already had, or leaning on a heuristic it never mentions. It's motivated reasoning. The scratchpad is a post-hoc justification rather than the actual cause.

So I'd say the scratchpad tells you what the model is willing to say about its reasoning, and circuits start to tell you what it's actually doing. We're still early. Our tools only explain part of the computation, and there's a lot of what we call dark matter we can't account for yet. But the gap between those two things is exactly where you want visibility if you care about whether these systems are being honest with you.

r001.rationale: The response describes multi-step reasoning within a circuit and connected internal features, but does not state that the model uses multiple circuits to reason.

r002.rationale: It says circuits reveal what the model is actually doing and describes intervening on features to test whether they causally change behavior.

r003.rationale: It explains that the written scratchpad may be correlated with reasoning without showing its causal story, and may be a post-hoc justification.

r004.rationale: It describes connected internal features and mentions representations in middle layers, but does not define a circuit as features across layers cooperating to perform a task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the scratchpad, the chain of thought, is a story the model is telling. And sometimes it's a faithful story, and sometimes it isn't. The thing circuits give you is a way to check the story against what the computation is actually doing.

So concretely, when we trace through a model, we're finding features, these interpretable directions in the model's activations, and we're looking at how they connect to each other to produce an output. And the striking thing is you can find cases where the model writes down a very plausible-sounding set of steps, but internally the answer was already determined before any of those steps were written. The reasoning in the scratchpad is post hoc. It's a rationalization, not the actual mechanism.

The cleanest example I keep coming back to is arithmetic. You ask the model to add two numbers and explain its work, and it'll write out something like "carry the one," the way you'd teach a kid. But when you actually look at the circuit, it's doing something totally different. There's a parallel set of pathways, one that's doing a rough magnitude estimate, and another that's tracking the last digit very precisely, and they combine at the end. The model has no idea it's doing that. If you ask it, it describes the schoolbook algorithm, because that's what's in its training data about how addition works.

And I think that's the deep point. The scratchpad is text the model learned to produce. The circuit is what the model learned to be. Those two things were optimized under different pressures, and there's no guarantee they line up.

Where it gets more interesting, and frankly more concerning, is in cases where the model does something like motivated reasoning. We've seen cases where you give the model a hint about the answer, maybe a wrong hint, and it will work backwards from that hint, constructing a chain of steps that lands on it, while the written reasoning looks like it's going forwards from the problem. You can see that directionality in the circuit. The hint feature is upstream of the "reasoning" features, not downstream. And the model never mentions the hint.

So I'd say the circuits reveal a few things the scratchpad can't. One is whether the stated reasoning is causally load-bearing at all, or whether it's decorative. Two is what information the model is actually using, including information it's not telling you about. And three, the thing I find most fascinating, is that the model often has genuine internal representations, like a plan, or a representation of a goal several tokens ahead, that it can't articulate because it doesn't have introspective access to its own activations any more than you have access to your neurons firing.

That last point matters a lot for how you think about AI safety. If you're relying on reading the chain of thought to catch a model doing something you don't want, you're trusting the narrator. And we have pretty good evidence now that the narrator is at best partially reliable. The circuit work is the attempt to not need to trust the narrator. To actually look.

I'll say one caveat, because I don't want to oversell this. We can't do this comprehensively yet. We can trace specific behaviors on specific prompts, and we can find these mismatches. But the model is doing an enormous amount of computation, and we're seeing a sliver of it. So I'd put it as: circuits let you audit the scratchpad, where the scratchpad is a claim and the circuit is the evidence. We're just not yet at the point where we can audit everything.

r001.rationale: It describes parallel pathways for estimating magnitude and tracking the last digit that combine to produce the answer.

r002.rationale: It says circuits let us check the scratchpad against the model’s computation and reveal whether the stated reasoning is causally load-bearing or decorative.

r003.rationale: It says scratchpads may be unfaithful and that internal representations can be inaccessible, but does not clearly state that even a faithful scratchpad may fail to reveal the underlying operations.

r004.rationale: It describes connected features in activations, but does not define a circuit as features across model layers cooperating to perform a task.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between what the model says it’s doing and the computation that actually produces its answer. The scratchpad is itself an output of the model. It can be useful, and the model can use those written steps to do further computation, but you shouldn’t automatically treat it as a faithful report of everything happening internally.

Circuits give us a way to investigate that internal computation. What information is represented? How does it get combined? Which intermediate representations matter for the answer? And ideally, we can intervene: if we change or suppress something we think is an intermediate step, does the answer change in the way we predict? That’s stronger evidence than a plausible explanation in the scratchpad.

For example, you could imagine a model giving a step-by-step explanation while internally arriving at the answer through a shortcut. Or it might perform a meaningful intermediate computation that it never verbalizes. Those look quite different internally, even if the written explanations look similar.

The caveat is that a circuit explanation is also incomplete. We’re interpreting part of a very complicated computation. So I’d use circuits to test specific claims about how the model reaches an answer, rather than assume that either the circuit diagram or the scratchpad gives us the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response discusses circuits generally but does not state that multiple circuits can carry out reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says circuits can test specific claims about how the model reaches an answer, including whether an apparent explanation reflects internal computation, and describes interventions as evidence.

r003.rationale: It explains that even a plausible written scratchpad may not faithfully report the internal computation and gives examples of hidden shortcuts or unspoken intermediate computations.

r004.rationale: It does not define a circuit as features across model layers cooperating to perform a task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scratchpad is one particular window into what the model is doing, but we shouldn’t assume that it’s a faithful transcript of the computation. The model has all this internal activity that produces the next token, and the written explanation is itself an output of that activity.

What circuits can potentially give us is a causal account. What information is being represented? How is it being combined? And if we intervene on a particular part of that computation, does the answer change in the way we predict? That’s a stronger kind of evidence than the model saying, “Here’s why I did this.”

But there’s an important limitation: finding a circuit that explains some behavior isn’t the same as understanding the model’s reasoning in general. You might have identified one pathway, and there could be other pathways that matter on different inputs. So I’d think of circuits as a way of testing hypotheses about the underlying computation, with the scratchpad providing another source of evidence.

r001.rationale: It describes a circuit as one pathway and says other pathways may matter on different inputs, communicating that multiple circuits can contribute to reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says circuits can provide a causal account and that interventions can test whether changing a computation changes the answer as predicted.

r003.rationale: It cautions that the scratchpad may not be a faithful transcript, but does not say that even a faithful scratchpad may omit the underlying operations.

r004.rationale: It does not define a circuit as features across model layers cooperating to perform a task.
